content.text:
I submitted **index 62** (Fe 0.39, Ni 0.18, V 0.42) as the best composition. It gave the highest photocurrent of the three I could measure: **7.5e-7 A**.

| Index | Composition (Fe / Ni / V) | Photocurrent | Why I picked it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **62** | 0.39 / 0.18 / 0.42 | **7.5e-7 A** | Similar Fe and V with little Ni, like FeVO4, which should absorb the 2.72 eV (455 nm) light |
| 159 | 0.58 / 0.22 / 0.20 | 5.3e-7 A | To compare against the Fe-rich end |
| 90 | 0.34 / 0.17 / 0.48 | 5.3e-7 A | To test adding more V to the low-Ni region |

- **Confidence is low.** The library has 160 compositions and the budget allowed only 3 merit measurements. The two points on either side of 62 both came in lower, but that's too little to call 62 the library's best. The areas with more Ni were never measured.
- **The model predictions didn't help rank anything.** Each merit measurement first required a band-gap prediction, and I only ever ran one for hematite (Fe2O3). Depending on the method, it came out anywhere from 0.8 to 2.8 eV, too inconsistent to use. I recorded the predictions as uninformative, and my choices came from general knowledge of Fe-V oxides and the measured trend.
- **I didn't use the 5 XRD measurements.** They could have checked whether the samples near 62 actually contain an FeVO4-like phase.
- **I never read the full list of known phases.** It was too large to return directly, and I had no tool to open the saved file.
